Section 6.2 of Lock⁵ turns the simulations of Chapter 4 into formulas. For
inference about a population mean $\mu$ we no longer need a randomization
or bootstrap distribution on screen: the **standard error for a sample mean**
has a formula,
$$SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},$$
and because $s$ (the sample standard deviation) is only an *estimate* of the
unknown $\sigma$, the standardized statistic
$$t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$$
follows a **$t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom** rather than a
standard normal — a slightly heavier-tailed curve that charges a small
penalty for not knowing $\sigma$. The same curve powers both tasks of this
section. A **confidence interval for a mean** is
$\bar x \pm t^*\cdot s/\sqrt{n}$, where $t^*$ is the endpoint of a
$t$-distribution with $n-1$ df holding the desired confidence (for 95%,
$t^*=2.052$ at $n=28$ vs the normal $z^*=1.96$; the gap shrinks as $n$
grows). A **t-test** for $H_0\colon \mu=\mu_0$ computes $t$ and reads the
p-value as a tail area (one tail or two) of $T_{n-1}$. The t-tools are
valid when the population is reasonably normal, or when the sample is
large ($n\ge 30$), where the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling
distribution of $\bar x$ nearly normal even for skewed populations — so a
skewed dotplot only rules out $t$ when the sample is small or carries
extreme outliers, in which case we fall back on bootstrap methods. A final
formula answers the design question: to achieve a margin of error $ME$ at
a given confidence level, collect about $n=(z^*\tilde\sigma/ME)^2$
observations, where $\tilde\sigma$ is a pre-study guess at the population
standard deviation. Below we compute every endpoint, interval, and p-value
exactly with `scipy.stats.t`, and, wherever the exercise references a real
Lock⁵ dataset, we load the data and verify the formula answer against a
bootstrap or randomization simulation (10000 resamples, seed 2026). The
exercises are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd
ed., pp. 452–468): 6.65–6.88 build the $SE = s/\sqrt{n}$ and
$t$-distribution skills; 6.89–6.125 work t-intervals and sample-size
planning; 6.126–6.142 run full t-tests, from body temperature and
Deflategate to mercury in Florida lakes.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def se_mean(s, n):
    """SE for a sample mean: s / sqrt(n)."""
    return s / np.sqrt(n)

def t_endpoint(n, tail):
    """Endpoint of a t-distribution (df = n-1) with `tail` probability beyond each end."""
    return float(stats.t.ppf(1 - tail, n - 1))

def t_area(value, n, side):
    """Area of a t-distribution (df = n-1) above or below a value."""
    df = n - 1
    return float(stats.t.sf(value, df) if side == "above" else stats.t.cdf(value, df))

def t_ci(xbar, s, n, conf, digits=3):
    """t-interval for a mean: best estimate, t*, SE, margin of error, interval."""
    df = n - 1
    se = s / np.sqrt(n)
    tstar = float(stats.t.ppf(0.5 + conf / 2, df))
    me = tstar * se
    return pd.Series({"Best estimate": round(float(xbar), digits),
                      "t* (df=%d)" % df: round(tstar, 3),
                      "SE": round(float(se), 4),
                      "Margin of error": round(float(me), digits),
                      "%d%% CI" % round(100 * conf): f"({round(xbar - me, 2)}, {round(xbar + me, 2)})"})

def t_test(xbar, s, n, mu0, tail, digits=4):
    """One-row t-test for a mean: statistic, t, df, p-value."""
    df = n - 1
    se = s / np.sqrt(n)
    t = (xbar - mu0) / se
    p = (float(stats.t.sf(t, df)) if tail == "right"
         else float(stats.t.cdf(t, df)) if tail == "left"
         else float(2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df)))
    return pd.Series({"Sample mean": round(float(xbar), 3),
                      "Null mean": mu0,
                      "SE": round(float(se), 4),
                      "t-statistic": round(float(t), 3),
                      "df": df,
                      "p-value": round(p, digits)})

def t_curve(tstat, df, tail, figsize=(6, 2.6)):
    """t-distribution with the p-value tail(s) beyond tstat shaded."""
    x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 500)
    y = stats.t.pdf(x, df)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.plot(x, y, color="#4c72b0", lw=2)
    if tail == "right":
        mask = x >= tstat
    elif tail == "left":
        mask = x <= tstat
    else:
        mask = (x >= abs(tstat)) | (x <= -abs(tstat))
    if mask.any():
        ax.fill_between(x[mask], y[mask], color="#c44e52", alpha=0.65)
    ax.axvline(np.clip(tstat, -5, 5), color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("t")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def boot_means(data, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Bootstrap distribution of the sample mean: `reps` resamples of the data."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    data = np.asarray(data, float)
    idx = r.integers(0, len(data), (reps, len(data)))
    return data[idx].mean(axis=1)

def rand_means(data, null, reps=10000, seed=2026):
    """Randomization distribution for a mean under H0: shift the data so the
    sample mean equals the null value, then resample."""
    data = np.asarray(data, float)
    return boot_means(data - data.mean() + null, reps, seed)

def tail_plot(boots, observed, tail, xlabel, null=0.0, bins=40, figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of a simulated distribution with the p-value tail shaded."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=boots, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    if tail == "right":
        mask = boots >= observed
    elif tail == "left":
        mask = boots <= observed
    else:
        mask = np.abs(boots - null) >= abs(observed - null)
    if mask.any():
        sns.histplot(x=boots[mask], bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#c44e52")
    ax.axvline(observed, color="black", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Simulated statistics")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def p_row(label, stat, boots, tail, null=0.0, digits=4):
    """One-row summary: statistic and simulation p-value."""
    if tail == "right":
        p = (boots >= stat).mean()
    elif tail == "left":
        p = (boots <= stat).mean()
    else:
        p = (np.abs(boots - null) >= abs(stat - null)).mean()
    return pd.Series({label: round(float(stat), 4),
                      "Simulation p-value": round(float(p), digits),
                      "Simulated samples": len(boots)})

def dotplot(vals, xlabel, figsize=(6, 1.6)):
    """Dotplot of a small sample."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.stripplot(x=np.asarray(vals, float), ax=ax, color="#4c72b0",
                  size=8, jitter=False, alpha=0.75)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def sample_n(me, conf, sigma):
    """Sample size for a desired margin of error: n = (z* sigma-hat / ME)^2, rounded up."""
    z = float(stats.norm.ppf(0.5 + conf / 2))
    return int(np.ceil((z * sigma / me) ** 2))
```

## Exercise 6.65

*(Skill Builder 1)* Samples of size $n = 1000$ from a population with mean
28 and standard deviation 5: find the SE of the distribution of sample means.

```{python}
#| echo: false
round(se_mean(5, 1000), 3)
```

$$SE=\sigma/\sqrt{n}=5/\sqrt{1000}\approx 0.158$$ — with 1000 observations
the sample means vary by only about 0.16 around the true mean of 28.

## Exercise 6.77

**Impact of Sample Size on Accuracy.** Compute the SE for sample means from
a population with $\mu = 100$, $\sigma = 25$, for $n = 30, 200, 1000$;
discuss the effect of increasing $n$ on the SE and on the accuracy of
$\bar x$ as an estimator of $\mu$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Standard error of the sample mean versus sample size for a population with sigma = 25
ns = np.arange(5, 1000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
ax.plot(ns, 25 / np.sqrt(ns), color="#4c72b0", lw=2)
for n0 in (30, 200, 1000):
    ax.plot(n0, 25 / np.sqrt(n0), "o", color="#c44e52")
    ax.annotate(f"n={n0}: SE={25/np.sqrt(n0):.2f}", (n0, 25 / np.sqrt(n0)),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 4), fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Sample size n")
ax.set_ylabel("SE = 25 / sqrt(n)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
pd.Series({"SE at n=30": round(se_mean(25, 30), 3),
           "SE at n=200": round(se_mean(25, 200), 3),
           "SE at n=1000": round(se_mean(25, 1000), 3)}).to_string()
```

The SEs are 4.56, 1.77, and 0.79: increasing the sample size decreases the
standard error like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so the curve above falls steeply at first
and then flattens. Consequences: larger samples give more accurate estimates
of $\mu$ (sample means cluster more tightly around 100), but with diminishing
returns — to *halve* the SE you must *quadruple* $n$ (going from SE 4.56 at
$n=30$ to 1.77 needs more than a sixfold increase in $n$).

## Exercise 6.78

**Impact of the Population Standard Deviation on SE.** Same population mean
$\mu = 100$, sample size $n = 100$, but $\sigma = 5, 25, 75$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"SE when sigma = 5": se_mean(5, 100),
           "SE when sigma = 25": se_mean(25, 100),
           "SE when sigma = 75": se_mean(75, 100)}).to_string()
```

The SEs are 0.5, 2.5, and 7.5 — **directly proportional to $\sigma$**
(they equal $\sigma/10$ here). More variability in the population means more
variability in sample means and less accuracy for $\bar x$; a fifteen-fold
increase in $\sigma$ multiplies the SE fifteen-fold.

## Exercise 6.79

**Is a t-distribution appropriate?** A sample with $n = 12$, $\bar x = 7.6$,
$s = 1.6$; the dotplot (p. 453) runs from 5 to 11 with a single main hump and
no extreme outliers.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"t appropriate?": "Yes",
           "df": 12 - 1,
           "SE = s/sqrt(n)": round(se_mean(1.6, 12), 3)}).to_string()
```

**Yes** — the dotplot shows a single, roughly symmetric cluster with no
outliers, so treating the population as reasonably normal is plausible for
this modest sample. Use $t$ with **df $= 11$** and **SE $= 1.6/\sqrt{12}
\approx 0.462$**.

## Exercise 6.80

**Is a t-distribution appropriate?** A sample with $n = 75$, $\bar x =
18.92$, $s = 10.1$; the dotplot is clearly right-skewed, stretching out
toward 60.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"t appropriate?": "Yes",
           "df": 75 - 1,
           "SE = s/sqrt(n)": round(se_mean(10.1, 75), 3)}).to_string()
```

**Yes** — the skew would be a problem for a small sample, but
$n = 75 \ge 30$ is large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to make the
distribution of sample means approximately normal, so the t-tools are fine.
Use $t$ with **df $= 74$** and **SE $= 10.1/\sqrt{75} \approx 1.166$**.

## Exercise 6.81

**Is a t-distribution appropriate?** A sample with $n = 18$, $\bar x =

scattered down to 60.


**No.** The dotplot is clearly skewed left and $n = 18 < 30$ is not large
enough for the CLT to rescue the t-tools. (If we used $t$ anyway it would
have df $= 17$ and SE $= 10.6/\sqrt{18} \approx 2.50$, but the safe route is
to build a **bootstrap** confidence interval instead.)

## Exercise 6.82

**Is a t-distribution appropriate?** A sample with $n = 10$, $\bar x =
508.5$, $s = 21.5$; the dotplot huddles near 505–510 with isolated points
near 535 and 565–570.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"t appropriate?": "No",
           "df (would be)": 10 - 1,
           "SE would be": round(se_mean(21.5, 10), 3)}).to_string()
```

**No.** With only $n = 10$ observations and two visible high outliers, the
population cannot be considered normal — the outliers both inflate $s$ and
wreck the normality condition. (Mechanically $t$ would have df $= 9$ and SE
$= 21.5/\sqrt{10} \approx 6.80$, but a **bootstrap** interval is the
appropriate tool.)

## Exercise 6.84

**Advise a Fellow Student.** *My population is pretty right-skewed, but I am
taking a large sample of 200 cases, so it is safe to assume the sample is
normally distributed.*

Discussion — no computation. The student has the right conclusion for the
wrong reason. With $n = 200$ from a skewed population, the **sample itself**
will look just as right-skewed as the population — it is *not* normally
distributed, and no sample size changes that. What *is* true is that the
**sampling distribution of the sample mean** becomes approximately normal
for large $n$ by the Central Limit Theorem, so t-inference about the *mean*
($\bar x \pm t^*s/\sqrt{n}$ or a t-test) is safe. The advice: do not claim
the data are normal; claim the *distribution of $\bar x$* is approximately
normal, which is the condition the t-tools actually need.

## Exercise 6.85

**College SAT Samples.** Suppose AvgSAT (mean combined SAT of four-year
colleges) is fairly bell-shaped with $\mu = 1135$ and $\sigma = 130$.
(a) Sketch the population distribution; (b) sketch the distribution of
$\bar x$ for repeated samples of $n = 100$ colleges.

*Data check:* `data/ch02/CollegeScores4yr.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CollegeScores4yr.csv> (its 1277
colleges with AvgSAT have mean 1135 and SD 129 — consistent with the
supposed values):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Population distribution of AvgSAT and the sampling distribution of the mean for samples of 100 colleges
x = np.linspace(700, 1570, 600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.8))
ax.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, 1135, 130), color="#4c72b0", lw=2, label="Population: N(1135, 130)")
ax.plot(x, stats.norm.pdf(x, 1135, 13), color="#c44e52", lw=2,
        label="Sample means, n=100: N(1135, 13)")
ax.set_xlabel("AvgSAT")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
cs = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/CollegeScores4yr.csv")
sat = cs.AvgSAT.dropna()
pd.Series({"AvgSAT n": len(sat), "mean": round(sat.mean(), 1),
           "sd": round(sat.std(), 1),
           "(b) SE for n = 100": se_mean(130, 100)}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** A normal curve centered at 1135 with SD 130 (blue curve above).
- **(b)** By the CLT, the sample means follow $N(1135,\ 130/\sqrt{100}) =
  N(1135,\ 13)$ (red curve): the **same center**, but one-tenth the spread.

## Exercise 6.87

**AvgSAT over 1180?** Continuing Exercise 6.85 with $N(1135, 130)$ and
$n = 100$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"(a) P(AvgSAT over 1180), one college": round(float(stats.norm.sf(1180, 1135, 130)), 4),
           "(b) P(xbar over 1180), n = 100": float(f"{stats.norm.sf(1180, 1135, 13):.2e}")}).to_string()
```

- **(a)** $z = (1180 - 1135)/130 = 0.35$: about **36.5%** of colleges have
  AvgSAT of 1180 or higher.
- **(b)** $z = (1180 - 1135)/13 = 3.46$: only about **0.0003** (3 in 10000)
  samples of 100 colleges average 1180 or higher — averaging 100 colleges
  shrinks the spread ten-fold, so a sample mean that far above 1135 is rare.
- **(c)** If AvgSAT were actually right-skewed: part **(a) would no longer
  be appropriate** (it assumes the population itself is normal), but part
  **(b) would still be fine** — with $n = 100$ the CLT makes the
  distribution of $\bar x$ approximately normal even for a skewed
  population, as long as the stated $\mu$ and $\sigma$ hold.

## Exercise 6.92

*(Skill Builder 1)* 90% t-interval from $\bar x = 137.0$, $s = 53.9$,

## Exercise 6.109

**Bright Light at Night Makes Even Fatter Mice.** The $n = 9$ mice with a
bright light on all the time gained $\bar x = 11.0$ g with $s = 2.6$;
Figure 6.10 shows a cluster near 10 with a clear outlier near 18 g. Is a
t-distribution appropriate? If not, how else might we build the interval?

Discussion — no computation. **Not appropriate.** The sample is tiny
($n = 9$) and the dotplot shows a distinct high outlier at about 18 g, so
the population cannot be considered normal and the CLT offers no help at
this size. The outlier also inflates $s$, making any formula interval
misleading. Instead we should use **bootstrap methods** (Chapter 3):
resample the 9 mice thousands of times and take percentiles of the bootstrap
distribution of means as the confidence interval.

## Exercise 6.110

**United Flights in December.** Computer output for the difference in
actual vs scheduled arrival time of $n = 1000$ United December flights:
Mean $= 4.21$, StDev $= 45.34$, SE Mean $= 1.43$, Min $= -51$, Q1 $= -15$,
Median $= -5$, Q3 $= 8$, Max $= 872$.

*Data:* `data/ch04/DecemberFlights.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/DecemberFlights.csv> (United rows
reproduce the output exactly):

```{python}
#| echo: false
dec = pd.read_csv("data/ch04/DecemberFlights.csv")
u = dec.loc[dec.Airline == "United", "Difference"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
pd.Series({"n": len(u), "mean": round(u.mean(), 2),
           "sd": round(u.std(ddof=1), 2),
           "SE": round(u.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(u)), 2),
           "min": u.min(), "Q1": np.percentile(u, 25),
           "median": np.median(u), "Q3": np.percentile(u, 75),
           "max": u.max()}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Boxplot of the difference between actual and scheduled arrival times for 1000 United flights in December
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.2))
sns.boxplot(x=u, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("Actual minus scheduled arrival time (minutes)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
t_ci(4.21, 45.34, 1000, 0.95).to_string()
```

- **(a)** The sample mean difference is **4.21 minutes** (flights arrive
  4.21 minutes late on average); the standard deviation of the differences
  is **45.34 minutes**.
- **(b) No.** The median ($-5$) is well below the mean (4.21) and the max
  (872) dwarfs Q3 (8) — the output shows strong right skew with extreme
  outliers, so this sample is not normally distributed.
- **(c) Yes, we can proceed.** The t-tools require a *normal sampling
  distribution of the mean*, not normal data: with $n = 1000$ the CLT
  applies, and even the 872-minute outlier has little influence on a mean
  of 1000 values.
- **(d)** $4.21 \pm 1.962 \cdot 1.43 = 4.21 \pm 2.81 = \textbf{(1.40,
  7.02)}$ minutes.
- **(e)** We are 95% sure that United flights in December arrive, on
  average, between about 1.4 and 7.0 minutes later than scheduled.

```{python}
pd.Series({"ME = 10": sample_n(10, 0.95, 30),
           "ME = 5": sample_n(5, 0.95, 30),
           "ME = 1": sample_n(1, 0.95, 30)}).to_string()
```

The required sizes are **35, 139, and 3458**. Since $n = (z^*\tilde\sigma/ME)^2$,
halving the margin of error **quadruples** the sample size (35 → 139 → 554
→ ...): accuracy is expensive, and each extra digit of precision costs
disproportionately more.

## Exercise 6.122

**What influences the sample size needed?** Sample size for ME within
$\pm 3$ with 99%, 95%, and 90% confidence ($\tilde\sigma = 30$).

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"99% confidence": sample_n(3, 0.99, 30),
           "95% confidence": sample_n(3, 0.95, 30),
           "90% confidence": sample_n(3, 0.90, 30)}).to_string()
```

The required sizes are **664, 385, and 271**. Higher confidence demands a
wider net and hence a **larger** sample to keep the same margin of error —
from 90% to 99% confidence roughly raises $n$ by a factor of 2.5.

## Exercise 6.123

**What influences the sample size needed?** Sample size for ME within
$\pm 3$ (95% confidence) with $\tilde\sigma = 100, 50, 10$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"sigma-tilde = 100": sample_n(3, 0.95, 100),
           "sigma-tilde = 50": sample_n(3, 0.95, 50),
           "sigma-tilde = 10": sample_n(3, 0.95, 10)}).to_string()
```

The required sizes are **4269, 1068, and 43**. Since $n$ grows like
$\tilde\sigma^2$, each halving of the population variability quarters the
sample size needed — knowing the population is homogeneous is worth more
than any amount of extra data collection.

restaurant is between about 15.9% and 17.3%; the bootstrap interval

## Exercise 6.134

**Be Nice to Pigeons, as They Remember Your Face.** After training with a
hostile and a neutral person, $n = 32$ measurements of (pigeons at neutral
site minus hostile site) give $\bar x = 3.9$ with $s = 6.8$. Test whether
the mean difference is greater than zero.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: t-distribution with 31 df and the right tail beyond t = 3.24 shaded
t_curve(t_test(3.9, 6.8, 32, 0, "right")["t-statistic"], 31, "right")
t_test(3.9, 6.8, 32, 0, "right").to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distribution of the mean difference when the null mean is 0, observed 3.9 shaded in the right tail
```

$H_0\colon \mu = 0$ vs $H_a\colon \mu > 0$. $t = 3.9/1.202 = 3.24$,
df $= 31$, **p-value $\approx 0.0014$**; the randomization simulation above

$H_0$**: the data provide convincing evidence that more pigeons gather at
the neutral person's site — the birds recognize the hostile human's face
and remember the grudge.

**Homes for Sale.** Table 6.2 gives mean and SD of prices ($1000s) for

greater than 278? Which state shows the most evidence?

```{python}

homes = pd.DataFrame({"State": ["New York", "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania"],
                      "n": [30, 30, 30],
                      "Mean": [365.3, 328.5, 265.6],

homes.to_string(index=False)
```

```{python}

rows = [t_test(365.3, 317.8, 30, 278, "right"),
        t_test(328.5, 158.0, 30, 278, "right"),
        t_test(265.6, 137.1, 30, 278, "right")]
pd.DataFrame({"State": ["New York", "New Jersey", "Pennsylvania"],
              "t-statistic": [r["t-statistic"] for r in rows],
              "df": [r["df"] for r in rows],
              "p-value (H_a: mu > 278)": [r["p-value"] for r in rows]}).to_string(index=False)
```

- **(a) New York:** $t = (365.3 - 278)/58.0 = 1.51$, df $= 29$, p-value
  $\approx 0.072 > 0.05$ — **not significant**, despite the highest mean,
  because $s = 317.8$ makes the SE huge.

  $\approx 0.045 < 0.05$ — **significant** (barely).
- **(c) Pennsylvania:** $t = -12.4/25.0 = -0.50$, df $= 29$, p-value
  $\approx 0.688$ — **no evidence** (the sample mean is actually *below*
  278).
- **(d) New Jersey** shows the most evidence that its state average exceeds
  the national typical price: it pairs an above-average mean with moderate
  variability, while New York's enormous spread swamps its higher mean.

**Team Batting Average in Baseball.** From `BaseballHits2019` (all 30 MLB
teams in 2019, treated as a sample of all teams in all years): $N = 30$,

```{python}

pd.concat([t_test(0.25217, 0.01084, 30, 0.26, "two"),

```

  (0.24812, 0.25622) — identical to our hand-computed values (up to
  rounding of the fourth decimal), confirming the t-test procedure.
